<div class="split"><div><p class="eyebrow">CAP · Week 4</p>

# Orchestrating<br>AI agents

<p class="statement">Who keeps the work moving?</p></div><figure>

![A Human checking work coordinated by Agents][hero]

</figure></div>

<!--
Timing: 0:00–1:00.
Start with the connection to last week: we can already describe what we want and work with an agent. Today we change who handles the next step while we stay responsible for the result. We will build up from one conversation to a team and a separate program.
The illustrations show ideas, not actual product screenshots. All demo commands and prompts are in the separate runbooks.
-->

---

# It forgot my color

<p>Pick teal. Reload the page.<br>It’s navy again.</p>
<div class="paint">

![The app loses the selected teal color after reload][paint-fail]

</div>

<!--
Timing: 1:00–2:00.
Use a small, recognizable bug before naming any roles. Imagine a paint app that works while you use it, but forgets the selected color when the browser reloads. The app returns to navy. We want the tool and color to survive a reload. Each illustrated canvas shows a new stroke drawn after reload; preserving the canvas drawing is outside this feature.
These illustrations are examples of the behavior, not screenshots or evidence from our demo.
-->

---

# Our feature: remember my choices

<p>Same tool. Same color.<br>Bad saved data? Safe defaults.</p>
<div class="paint">

![The chosen teal color remains after reload][paint-pass]

</div>

<!--
Timing: 2:00–3:00.
Connect to spec-driven development. Agree on success before starting work: pencil or eraser, and a chosen color, should remain selected after reload. A teal pencil stroke after reload proves that color affects actual drawing. If saved data is broken, restore pencil and navy so drawing still works.
The illustration shows a new teal stroke drawn after reload, not a saved canvas. The coordinated demos use this same feature. The early improvement loop has a different purpose: grow a paint app from an empty folder and see how repeated sessions evolve it.
-->

---

# You guide one step at a time

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Human asks an Agent to build, then reviews the result and gives the next instruction."></div>
<p class="caption"><strong>In the loop:</strong> you choose each next step.</p>

<!--
Timing: 3:00–5:00.
This is the familiar in-the-loop approach: ask for one change, inspect the result, and give the next instruction. For our feature, you might ask for controls, then saving, then a reload check.
This gives close control and quick course correction. It also means you are the person connecting every step. An agent here means a model that can use tools and act on the project.
-->

---

# One agent gets a bigger playbook

<div class="split"><div><p>The same agent builds,<br>checks, and repairs.</p><p class="human"><b>On the loop:</b><br>You return at agreed checkpoints.</p></div><figure>

![One Agent follows a playbook while a Human checks the result][single]

</figure></div>

<!--
Timing: 5:00–7:00.
The human and agent agree on the feature, instructions, checks, and limits. The same conversation can then implement controls, save preferences, run checks, and try a repair. You inspect at agreed points, for example after an implementation and before accepting it. This is on-the-loop work with one agent.
A playbook can be repository instructions, a workflow skill, prompts, and surrounding tools or hooks. Instructions describe the intended behavior. A program or hook enforces only what its code actually checks.
Use this when one connected feature fits one conversation. The setup is simple, but that conversation has to carry planning, implementation, checking, and repair context.
Concrete example: one Codex or Claude Code session implements remembered paint preferences using an agreed feature spec and checks. Official capability sources: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/developer-commands?surface=cli ; https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview
-->

---

# A script can repeat the same request

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="A script starts one fresh Agent session at a time. Updated code and a ledger persist between passes."></div>
<p class="caption">Fresh conversation. Same evolving app.</p>

<!--
Timing: 7:00–9:00.
Now move repetition into a small program. Each pass launches a fresh coding-agent session with the same improvement request. It reads the current app and progress ledger, makes a useful improvement, and reports what it did and what it imagined next. The script checks the app, saves a screenshot, records a local checkpoint, and starts the next pass.
There is one active worker at a time. Each conversation starts fresh. The code and ledger are shared on disk, so the project continues evolving. Earlier chat history does not carry over. Screenshots document the progression; the worker in our runbook does not read previous screenshots.
The loop caps each pass at 1,000 changed application-code lines and caps the total passes. This is the repeated fresh-context loop often called a Ralph loop. Names vary; describe the mechanics rather than assuming the name proves an exact implementation.
Use it for repeated improvement with inspectable saved files. A stale or misleading ledger can send the next session in the wrong direction.
Concrete example: a Bash script calls a coding CLI in noninteractive mode, captures results with Playwright, and repeats. https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/non-interactive-mode
-->

---

# A check tells the loop when to stop

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="An Agent works on one task. A passing check advances to the next task, while a failure allows one more attempt before asking the Human."></div>
<p class="caption">Each task gets a clear finish and a retry limit.</p>

<!--
Timing: 9:00–11:00.
Change the question from “make another useful improvement” to “finish this one task.” For example, keep trying to remember the selected color until the reload check passes. A process exiting successfully is not enough. The separate check needs to prove the requested behavior.
The script can allow a second attempt with the check failure, then stop and ask the human. Passing lets the next task start. This is a task completion loop. Putting several such tasks in an ordered list creates a task queue.
Use this for a known sequence with clear checks. The next action is easy to inspect in code, but the rules can stall when the failure needs a new plan. Our prepared queue allows two attempts per task.
-->

---

# Some jobs can happen together

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Agreed tool and color choices feed two independent jobs. Controls and saved settings must both finish before combining and checking."></div>
<p class="caption">Agree on the choices before splitting the work.</p>

<!--
Timing: 11:00–13:00.
Our preference feature has two separate jobs: build the visible tool/color controls, and write the code that saves and loads those choices. They can run together after we agree on the shape and valid values of the settings. Combining them waits for both jobs.
This drawing of jobs and “must happen before” arrows is a task graph. A fork shows jobs that can run together. A join shows work that waits for both. People also call an acyclic dependency graph a DAG. We do not need the abbreviation to understand the order.
In the demos, the UI worker edits toolbar.js, the settings worker edits settings.js, and an integration responsibility connects both through main.js. This reduces direct overlap but does not automatically make their results compatible.
-->

---

# A task graph

<div style="margin: 2px 0 12px;"><img alt="Shared API contract fans out to iOS app, Android app, Service X and Service Y; all join at Integration, which fans out to Mobile code review and Service code review; both join at Release approval" style="display:block;width:100%;height:390px;object-fit:contain" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," /></div>

<p class="muted">Boxes are tasks. Arrows mean “finish this first.”</p>
<p class="caption">A task starts after the jobs pointing to it finish.</p>

<!--
Use the minute already assigned to the preceding parallel-work example; keep the hour's agenda unchanged.
Read from left to right. Imagine adding shared account preferences across a mobile product: agree on an API contract, then let iOS, Android, Service X, and Service Y implement their parts in parallel. Service X can own preferences and Service Y can own accounts. These boxes name jobs, not agents or sessions.
Fan out means several jobs can become ready together. Integration waits for all four incoming jobs and combines their outputs; a join is a dependency barrier, not necessarily a Git merge. Integration can include checks that the pieces work together.
Then fan out again: review the mobile code and service code at the same time. Release approval waits for both reviews to pass. A box can be done by an agent, a script, or a person; the amber approval box is the human decision. A failed job keeps dependent jobs waiting until it is resolved.
This larger graph illustrates the pattern. The classroom paint-app demo uses a smaller graph.
-->

---

# Who chooses what happens next?

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="An Agent reads reports and chooses the next action. A Program follows explicit rules."></div>
<p class="caption">A system can use both.</p>

<!--
Timing: 13:00–16:00.
The useful distinction is who makes the coordination decision. A supervising agent can read a worker report, decide it is incomplete, and choose a different repair. A program can say: start ready tasks, run the named check, allow one retry, then stop.
The agent supplies judgment but can misunderstand a report. The program follows inspectable rules but cannot handle every surprise unless that response has been written. A program may call an agent for judgment when a rule says help is needed.
Both still run model-backed workers for coding. “Program control” does not mean the work has no model calls. It means routine ordering and watching can happen without asking a model what to do every time.
-->

---

# Two small scripts, two different goals

<div class="two-col"><div><h2>Improve again</h2><p>Same request each pass.</p><p class="muted">Watch the app evolve.</p></div><div><h2>Finish this task</h2><p>Repeat until its check passes.</p><p class="muted">Then start the next task.</p></div></div><p class="demo rule">Prepared runs: script, ledger, screenshots.</p>

<!--
Timing: 16:00–20:00.
Show the actual small scripts and saved progression from [Demo 1](demo-01-loop.md) and [Demo 1B](demo-01b-task-queue.md). Prepare both before class. Do not wait for 100 iterations during the hour.
Demo 1 starts with an empty paint-app folder and asks for the next useful improvement. It has an iteration limit. The app evolves cumulatively; these are not 100 unrelated branches. Show actual screenshots and the ledger from the run you prepared.
Demo 1B starts from a fixture and follows three ordered tasks implementing the agreed preferences. Each task has a behavior check and two attempts. Explain what made the queue move or stop using actual logs. If no automatic repair occurred, label any walkthrough as an expected path rather than a result.
Transition: a script works well when we can write down the next step. What changes when the next step needs judgment?
-->

# A main agent can run a team

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="The Human talks to a main Agent. The main Agent gives separate UI and saved-settings jobs to Workers, reads their reports, and owns combining and checking."></div>
<p class="caption"><strong>Supervisor:</strong> the main agent chooses assignments.</p>

<!--
Timing: 20:00–32:00.
20:00–24:00: introduce Supervisor as a name for this responsibility. You still talk to one main agent. It gives a clear UI job to one worker and a saved-settings job to another, reads their reports, and owns combining and checking the result. A separate reviewer can challenge the finished feature.
Each worker needs enough context to finish: what to do, which files to edit, how to check success, and when to stop. The main agent needs to receive real reports rather than merely tell a story about workers. Here separate worker sessions have their own context.
Use a supervising agent when task choice or repair needs judgment. Coordination adds model calls and the supervisor can make mistakes. Many systems also let the human steer the main conversation while workers run.
24:00–32:00: [Demo 2](demo-02-supervisor.md) is the live native-agent demonstration. The supplied default uses Codex. The lesson is independent of that product. Runbook compatibility instructions explain the Claude path if available. Show actual workers, their reports, integration, and review. Say what was observed and what remains unfinished.
Official examples: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents ; https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
-->

# Planning and running can be separate

<div class="split"><div><p><strong>Planner</strong><br>Helps you choose the work.</p><p><strong class="program">Controller</strong><br>A program runs the agreed steps.</p></div><figure>

![Human and Planner converse beside a separate Controller program running Workers][external]

</figure></div>

<!--
Timing: 32:00–35:00.
Give the two names only after the responsibilities are clear. The Planner is an agent you brainstorm with. It helps write the product requirements and task graph. The Controller is a separate program that starts ready jobs, watches state, checks results, and records progress.
The amber figure is you. The teal person beside you is the planning agent. The navy cabinet represents the program, and the teal people to the right are workers. The next slide makes the handoff explicit.
A real example is Gas City: configured planning agents use formulas that materialize as stored task graphs. Its external orchestrator advances control records while agents do work records. Our live classroom demo uses a small custom controller rather than installing Gas City.
Use this when execution should continue independently of the planning conversation. The extra setup must keep the agreed plan and running state aligned.
https://docs.gascity.com/getting-started/how-gas-city-works ; https://docs.gascity.com/getting-started/coming-from-gastown
-->

---

# You can keep talking while work runs

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="Human and Planner continue chatting while a separate Controller program follows the agreed plan, starts Workers, and sends a notification only when needed."></div>
<p class="caption">The program follows rules and calls agents for tasks.</p>

<!--
Timing: 35:00–44:00.
35:00–38:00: walk through the handoff. You and the Planner agree on the feature and inspect the task graph. The Controller validates that plan, starts the ready jobs, and records their status. The planning conversation stays available for a new idea or a status question. A future idea does not silently change the running plan.
The Controller can send a notification when work completes or needs help. It still calls agents to code and can call an agent to judge a repair. Routine watching and choosing ready jobs follow program rules.
38:00–44:00: [Demo 3](demo-03-external-controller.md) is the live separate-controller demonstration. The default CLI worker is Codex. Show the Planner, Controller, and observer terminals, the approved task graph, the two parallel jobs, and the integration wait. Talk to the Planner about a future undo feature while the program runs the original preference feature.
The small controller is a teaching example with fixed task shapes and explicit limits. It is not a general distributed scheduler. Notifications depend on the CLI compatibility path in the runbook; use the documented manual fallback when needed.
https://docs.gascity.com/getting-started/how-gas-city-works
-->

# A failed check needs a clear route

<div class="flow"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="A failed check leads to one bounded repair. A passing retry continues; another failure goes to the Human."></div>
<p class="caption">Keep the original goal. Limit repair attempts.</p>

<!--
Timing: 44:00–48:00.
Continue [Demo 3](demo-03-external-controller.md) at its labeled prepared failure checkpoint. The UI expects “color,” while the prepared settings defect returns “colour.” The real browser check exposes that mismatch. This is an intentionally inserted defect, not an observed model mistake.
The program detects failure. A fresh supervising agent reads the result and chooses either the permitted settings repair or a blocked handoff. A worker attempts that repair. The program checks again before continuing. If the configured attempt limit is reached, the human gets the failure and supporting output.
A useful repair route answers: who sees the failure, what may change, how many tries are allowed, and who gets called next? A repair should preserve the agreed feature and its original check.
-->

---

# We finish where we started

<p class="statement">Reload.<br>The same tool and color still work.</p><p class="rule">Broken saved data restores safe defaults.</p><p class="muted">Review the actual app and check results.</p>

<!--
Timing: 48:00–50:00.
Return to the concrete opening. Does a pencil stroke remain teal after reload? Does the eraser remain selected after reload and actually erase a newly drawn stroke? Does bad saved data restore pencil and navy? The canvas itself is not saved in these demos, so draw a fresh stroke after reload before checking erasing.
The reviewer checks the combined result. The human inspects actual behavior, check output, code changes, and remaining gaps. A worker saying “done” supports a decision but does not prove the feature works. Report partial or failed behavior honestly.
The final steps are in [Demo 3](demo-03-external-controller.md).
-->

---

# Each pattern has a job

| Pattern | Useful when | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| One playbook | One connected change | Context grows |
| Improve again | Explore from saved code | Can drift |
| Task queue | Clear task checks | Rules can stall |
| Main agent + workers | Next step needs judgment | Extra calls |
| Separate controller | Work continues outside chat | More setup |

<!--
Timing: 50:00–51:00.
These are control choices that can be combined. A single agent can use a script. A controller can ask a supervising agent for a repair. A main agent can delegate tasks that each run in a completion loop.
Choose the smallest arrangement that handles the actual dependencies and failures. Ask where the next decision lives, what proves success, and what makes the work stop. More agents do not automatically mean a better result.
-->

---

# Agents can also challenge a proposal

<div class="split"><div><p>One agent drafts the feature.</p><p>Another finds missing cases.</p><p class="human">You approve after a few rounds.</p></div><figure>

![Agents discuss one shared proposal while a Human decides whether to accept it][group]

</figure></div>

<!--
Timing: 51:00–52:00.
This is another useful pattern, often before implementation: a writer proposes the paint-preferences feature and a reviewer asks what happens after reload or when saved data is broken. The writer revises the same proposal. A turn limit keeps the discussion short, and the human approves the result.
Use it to challenge one idea from different perspectives. Extra discussion can cost time or go in circles, so define who speaks next and when to stop. Approval of the proposal does not prove the later code works.
Concrete technology example: Microsoft Agent Framework group chat has central speaker selection and a shared conversation. Its writer/reviewer example can be adapted to drafting and challenging this PRD. It is centrally coordinated discussion, not decentralized execution.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/orchestrations/group-chat
-->

<div class="two-col"><div><h2>A working app</h2><p>Three connected features.<br>Saved state.<br>One hard edge case.</p></div><div><h2>A real handoff</h2><p>Two responsibilities.<br>Someone combines the result.<br>Checks and clear stop points.</p></div></div><p class="muted rule">5–10 hours. Existing setups are welcome.</p>

<!--
Timing: 52:00–55:00.
Use [homework.md](homework.md) as the full assignment. Build a coherent paint app or another demanding editor for a target user and one complete workflow. The specification should include at least three interacting capabilities, saved and recoverable state, and a difficult edge case.
Choose an instruction workflow, script, existing orchestrator, or a combination. You need two distinct responsibilities and someone responsible for combining the result. They can run sequentially. Show an actual handoff, checks, time and retry limits, and the points where a human can intervene.
Submit the source and reproducible setup, product brief and acceptance results, workflow instructions or configuration, task responsibilities and dependency picture, selected logs, a product demo, and an explanation of what you trusted and checked. Label any deliberately inserted failure. You do not need to buy a product or build a production orchestrator.

# Appendix · Gas Town and Gas City

<div class="two-col"><div><h2>Gas Town</h2><p>Built-in coding roles.</p><p class="muted">Mayor coordinates.<br>Witness and Deacon watch lifecycles.<br>Refinery handles merges.</p></div><div><h2>Gas City</h2><p>Configured agents and workflows.</p><p class="muted">Planning produces stored tasks.<br>A program advances dependencies.<br>Agents perform the work.</p></div></div><p class="rule">Both mix agent judgment with program control.</p>

<!--
Appendix, outside the 60-minute main segment.
Gas Town provides an opinionated coding workflow with built-in roles and background controls. Gas City makes the familiar roles configurable through prompts, thresholds, and workflow formulas. Its formulas materialize as persisted task graphs; its orchestrator executes control records, while agents execute work records. Exact behavior depends on installed version and configuration.
Both let you combine interactive planning with agent execution and program services. The classroom separate-controller demo illustrates that separation with a much smaller custom program. It does not install or reproduce either product.
https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown ; https://docs.gascity.com/getting-started/coming-from-gastown ; https://docs.gascity.com/getting-started/how-gas-city-works
-->
